legal_principles.principle: The ends of justice should demand the transfer of the suit, appeal or other proceeding.
legal_principles.held: The cardinal principle for exercise of power under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that the ends of justice should demand the transfer of the suit, appeal or other proceeding.
cited_cases: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha
(2022) Live Law (SC) 627

legal_principles.principle: In matrimonial matters, the Courts have to take into consideration the economic soundness of both parties, social strata of spouses and their behavioural pattern.
legal_principles.held: In matrimonial matters, wherever Courts are called upon to consider the plea of transfer, the Courts have to take into consideration the economic soundness of both the parties, the social strata of the spouses and their behavioural pattern, their standard of life prior to the marriage and subsequent thereto and the circumstances of both the parties in eking out their livelihood and under whose protective umbrella they are seeking their sustenance to life.
applicable_acts_sections: Code of Civil Procedure — Section Y
cited_cases: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha
(2022) Live Law (SC) 627

legal_principles.principle: The Courts should give more weightage and consideration to the convenience of female litigants.
legal_principles.held: Further, when two or more proceedings are pending in different Courts between the same parties which raise common question of fact and law, and when the decisions in the cases are interdependent, it is desirable that they should be tried together by the same Judge so as to avoid multiplicity in trial of the same issues and conflict of decisions.
applicable_acts_sections: Code of Civil Procedure — Section X
cited_cases: Sumita Singh vs Kumar Sanjay

legal_principles.principle: The Courts should consider the family condition of the wife, custody of minor child, economic condition of the wife and her physical health.
legal_principles.held: Accordingly, it is well settled that while considering the transfer of a matrimonial dispute/case, at the instance of the wife, the Court is to consider the family condition of the wife, the custody of the minor child, economic condition of the wife, her physical health and earning capacity of the husband and most important the convenience of the wife i.e. she cannot travel alone without assistance of a male member of her family.
applicable_acts_sections: Code of Civil Procedure — Section Y
cited_cases: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha
(2022) Live Law (SC) 627

outcome.final_order: Petition for transfer allowed.

legal_principles.principle: The statutory period of six months specified in Section 13B(2) is directory in nature, but the power to waive it is subject to certain conditions.
legal_principles.held: Thus, it has been held that six months statutory period prescribed is directory in nature.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh (supra)

legal_principles.principle: The court should not grant permission for waiving off the stipulated period of six months under Section 13B(2) if the statutory period of one year under Section 13B is already over before the first motion itself.
legal_principles.held: In such circumstances, this Court cannot grant permission for waiving off the stipulated period of six months under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh (supra)

legal_principles.principle: The court should not grant permission for waiving off the stipulated period of six months under Section 13B(2) if all efforts for mediation/conciliation have failed and there is no likelihood of success in that direction by any further efforts.
legal_principles.held: Thus, it has been held that six months statutory period prescribed is directory in nature.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh (supra)

legal_principles.principle: The court should not grant permission for waiving off the stipulated period of six months under Section 13B(2) if the parties have genuinely settled their differences including alimony, custody of child or any other pending issues between the parties.
legal_principles.held: Thus, it has been held that six months statutory period prescribed is directory in nature.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh (supra)

outcome.final_order: The High Court's order dismissing the Civil Revisional Application was upheld, and the requirement to wait six months before filing the petition was not waived.

parties.respondent_defendant: Radha Arun and another (wife and alleged adulterer)

judgments.facts_of_case: The husband filed a petition under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, alleging adultery. The trial court allowed the petition.

legal_principles.principle: A person impleaded as a co-respondent in a petition under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, as alleged adulterer, cannot seek deletion on the ground that no relief is sought against him.
legal_principles.held: Once the petitioner chooses to implead as a co-respondent, the person who according to him is the adulterer, he being a proper party, cannot be deleted at the instance of such respondent.

legal_principles.principle: An adulterer is a proper, if not necessary party to a proceedings under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act.
legal_principles.held: The principles relating to impleading of parties make it clear that an adulterer is a proper, if not necessary party to a proceedings under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

outcome.final_order: The alleged adulterer is a proper party to the proceedings and cannot seek deletion from the petition.

legal_principles.held: We have heard the learned counsel for the appellant and the respondent. We have also gone through the pleadings, the evidence on record both documentary and oral recorded and impugned order passed by the Family Court.

legal_principles.principle: A party seeking to annul a marriage must establish the alleged fear and cessation of that fear before approaching the court.

legal_principles.principle: When interpreting a statute, specific provisions of the statute are to be read and understood in consistency with the language and intention of the said legal provisions.

legal_principles.principle: The caption of the Act or the Statement of Objects and Reasons or even the Preamble thereto cannot be used to construe a statute.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party challenging the vires of a statute to show that the statute is ultra vires.
legal_principles.held: It has to be borne in mind that while interpreting the statute, the specific provisions of statute are read and understood and have to be interpreted in consistence with the language and intention of the said legal provisions.

judgments.trial_court: Principal Family Court, Chennai, OP.SR.No.7428 of 2025
judgments.case_name: S.K.Ramya @ vs N.Ashwin Kumar
judgments.facts_of_case: The wife filed a divorce petition under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, which was returned by the trial court on jurisdictional grounds. The wife is currently residing in Sydney, Australia, but at the time of filing the petition, she was residing within the jurisdiction of the Family Court, Chennai.

legal_principles.principle: A Hindu who is domiciled in India can avail the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act, even if residing outside India.
legal_principles.held: Thus, the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act have extra territorial operation insofar as Hindus and it would be sufficient if the person who seeks relief or remedy under the Hindu Marriage Act to be domiciled in India.
cited_cases: Sondur Gopal vs. Sondur Rajini, (2013) 7 SCC 426

legal_principles.principle: Domicile can be domicile of origin or domicile of choice, and the Court should consider the specific averments in the petition.
legal_principles.held: Domicile can be domicile of origin or domicile of choice. Domicile of choice is where the person abandons one domicile and acquires residence in another domicile. Domicile of origin would prevail until another domicile is acquired by manifest abandonment of the domicile of origin.
cited_cases: S.K.Ramya @ vs N.Ashwin Kumar

outcome.final_order: The order of returns passed by the trial court is set aside and the petition is directed to be registered and assigned a main number on the file.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 2020 and had a child in 2021. The husband initiated divorce proceedings in Coimbatore, but the wife sought to transfer the case to Madurai due to difficulties in traveling from Madurai.

legal_principles.principle: Convenience of the wife should be given a superior consideration than that of husband in matters of transfer.
legal_principles.held: In line with this Parliamentary amendment, this Court and the Supreme Court have consistently held that convenience of wife should be given a superior consideration than that of husband.

legal_principles.principle: The Court should consider the difficulties faced by a wife in traveling to attend court proceedings.
legal_principles.held: As the distance between Madurai and Coimbatore is considerable and since it will be difficult for the wife to leave the child behind and travel to attend the Court, I am inclined to accept the transfer.

outcome.final_order: The court allowed the transfer petition and transferred the case to the Family Court, Madurai.

judgments.case_name: Vanaja vs Gopu
judgments.facts_of_case: Wife married husband in 1977, had a daughter, and lived together until 1984 when misunderstandings arose. Wife left husband's house and filed M.C. No. 9 of 1985 for maintenance, which was granted by the trial court at Rs. 250/- per mensem from 31.3.1986 onwards.

legal_principles.principle: A Hindu wife is entitled to be maintained by her husband during her lifetime.
legal_principles.held: Section 18(1) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, which came into operation on 21.12 1956, a Hindu wife, whether married before or after the commencement of that Act, shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her lifetime.
applicable_acts_sections: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act — Section 18

legal_principles.principle: The right to claim maintenance or litigation expenses under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act is a special statutory right.
legal_principles.held: It is thus clear that the right to claim maintenance or litigation expeneses under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, is not made available generally to the parties to a marriage, but only when a proceeding between the spouses is pending under that Act, and in that respect, the right conferred under Section 24 of that Act, is in the nature of a special statutory right not in any manner outside the provisions Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act.

outcome.final_order: Respondent should pay petitioner maintenance at the rate of Rs. 250/- per mensem from 31.3.1986 onwards, having regard to the income of the respondent.

judgments.case_name: Vijaykumar Ramchandra Bhate vs Neela Vijaykumar Bhate
judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 1973. The wife claimed dissolution of marriage under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The trial court allowed her petition. This is an appeal by the husband.

legal_principles.principle: A party's allegations of mental cruelty must be supported by cogent evidence.
legal_principles.held: The respondent has not examined a single independent witness in support of her case.

legal_principles.principle: A party's allegations of adultery must be supported by credible evidence.
legal_principles.held: There was no allegation that she had adulterous relations with him.

legal_principles.principle: A party's allegations of mental cruelty must not be sustained merely on the ground of petty quarrels.
legal_principles.held: The Family Court has held that petty quarrels between the appellant and the respondent were in the nature of ordinary wear and tear of the marital life, and did not amount to cruelty.

outcome.final_order: The respondent's petition for dissolution of marriage was allowed by the trial court, and this appeal is dismissed.

legal_principles.held: It is well settled that under Hindu Law the marriage of the minor is a voidable marriage at the instance of the minor.

legal_principles.principle: The consent of the petitioner or guardian must be obtained without force or fraud for a marriage to be valid.
legal_principles.held: This provision is applicable if the consent of the petitioner or the consent of the guardian of the petitioner was obtained by force or fraud.

legal_principles.principle: A marriage solemnized before a person attains the age of 15 years can be repudiated after attaining that age but before attaining the age of 18 years.
legal_principles.held: To attract this provision the marriage should have been solemnised before she attained the age of 15 years and she has to repudiate the marriage after attaining that age but before attaining the age of 18 years.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The trial court declared their marriage void under Section 12 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

legal_principles.principle: When a relationship of marriage is dissolved by decree of court and either no appeal is filed or if filed, is dismissed then either party to the marriage which has been dissolved by the process of law by a decree are free to marry again.
legal_principles.held: The phrase 'either party to the marriage' if is co-related with the first part of the section, marriage which has been dissolved by decree of divorce will indicate that what was provided in this section was that when a relationship of marriage is dissolved by decree of court and either no appeal is filed or if filed, is dismissed then either party to the marriage which has been dissolved by the process of law by a decree are free to marry again.

legal_principles.principle: The legislature so far as decrees under Section 13 are concerned wanted the right of appeal to survive but in decrees under Section 11 or 12 the legislature wanted the right of appeal to be subject to the will of the other party.
legal_principles.held: As it is apparent that if what is contended by the learned counsel for the respondent and held by some of the High Courts is accepted that Section 15 will not apply to cases when a decree is passed under Section 11 or 12 it will mean that as soon as a decree is passed the party aggrieved may appeal but the other party by remarriage would make the appeal infructuous and therefore the right of appeal of one of the parties to the decree under Section 28 will be subject to the act of the other party in cases where decree is passed under Section 11 or 12

outcome.final_order: The appeal was filed within time and the court set aside the order declaring the marriage void.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner seeks quashing of FIR No.478/2016 under Sections 498A/406/34 IPC. Parties settled on 17.08.2019, and marriage dissolved via mutual consent divorce decree dated 24.01.2020.

legal_principles.principle: The High Court may quash criminal proceedings if the parties have settled their disputes amicably, and there is hardly any likelihood of the offender being convicted.
legal_principles.held: However, certain offences which overwhelmingly and predominantly bear civil flavour having arisen out of civil, mercantile, commercial, financial, partnership or such like transactions or the offences arising out of matrimony, particularly relating to dowry, etc. or the family dispute, where the wrong is basically to the victim and the offender and the victim have settled all disputes between them amicably, irrespective of the fact that such offences have not been made compoundable, the High Court may within the framework of its inherent power, quash the criminal proceeding or criminal complaint or FIR if it is satisfied that on the face of such settlement, there is hardly any likelihood of the offender being convicted and by not quashing the criminal proceedings, justice shall be casualty and ends of justice shall be defeated.
cited_cases: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab & Another, (2012) 10 SCC 303
B.S. Joshi, (2003) 4 SCC 675; Nikhil Merchant, (2008) 9 SCC 677 and Manoj Sharma, (2008) 16 SCC 1.

legal_principles.principle: Courts should encourage genuine settlements of matrimonial disputes, particularly when they are on considerable increase.
legal_principles.held: Even if the offences are non-compoundable, if they relate to matrimonial disputes and the Court is satisfied that the parties have settled the same amicably and without any pressure, we hold that for the purpose of securing ends of justice, Section 320 of the Code would not be a bar to the exercise of power of quashing of FIR, complaint or the subsequent criminal proceedings.
cited_cases: Jitendra Raghuvanshi & Ors. Vs. Babita Raghuvanshi & Anr. (2013) 4 SCC 58

outcome.final_order: Exemption allowed, subject to just exceptions.

legal_principles.principle: The conduct of the respondent was not of such a character and gravity so as to give rise to a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the petitioner that it will be harmful or injurious for him to live with her or it would be impossible for them to live together without mental agony or torture.

legal_principles.principle: Parties to a marriage, tying nuptial knot, are supposed to bring about the union of two souls.
legal_principles.held: Parties to a marriage, tying nuptial knot, are supposed to bring about the union of two souls.

legal_principles.principle: Such ties cannot be allowed to be severed on the grounds/incidents or the conduct which on the face of it are ordinary wear and tear of matrimonial life.
legal_principles.held: Such ties cannot be allowed to be severed on the grounds/incidents or the conduct which on the face of it are ordinary wear and tear of matrimonial life.

judgments.facts_of_case: Marriage between Arun Pandey and Smt. Neha Pandey was solemnized on 23.01.2011. Out of the said wedlock, one son was born on 05.11.2015. The matrimonial relation became strained and due to indifference, the wife started living separately.

legal_principles.principle: A husband's obligation to maintain his wife arises on marriage, whereas such an obligation towards children arises on their birth.
legal_principles.held: These obligations are imposed on him by operation of law. It is also a moral obligation imposed upon him and it would rather be 'immoral' and 'illegal' to deny them maintenance.

legal_principles.principle: In a matrimonial proceeding, the wife and children are pitted against the husband or father, as the case may be, and in most of the cases they are not on equal footing.
legal_principles.held: Some gets financial support from their parents, brothers and sisters and also some work and earn, in exceptional cases. However, in all cases, the women and children are unable to face the onslaught of matrimonial proceedings because of their financial crisis, which tends to be exploited by the husbands.

legal_principles.principle: The object of Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act in providing maintenance to a party in matrimonial proceedings is obviously to provide financial assistance to the spouse to maintain himself or herself during the pendency of the proceedings and also to have sufficient funds to carry on the litigation so that the spouse does not unduly suffer in the conduct of the case for want of funds.
legal_principles.held: The said provision tends to create a fiction of equality, wherein the wife is tried to brought equally, at least financially along with the husband, so that the matrimonial case initiated is pursued by both the parties suitably & equally.

outcome.final_order: The respondent-wife is directed to pay Rs.50,000/- for legal activities (litigation expenses) and Rs.10,000/- as litigation costs, with a further direction to pay Rs.500/- per hearing within 30 days from the date of order.

judgments.facts_of_case: The petitioner's wife, Nidhi, was allegedly tortured by police officers. The report indicts the police and states that Nidhi was pressurised to implicate her husband and family members in a case of abduction and forcible marriage.

legal_principles.principle: Torture is not merely physical, but may also consist of mental and psychological torture calculated to create fright and submission to the demands or commands.
legal_principles.held: When the threats proceed from a person in Authority and that too by a police officer the mental torture caused by it is even more grave.

legal_principles.principle: Fabrication, illegal arrest, and detention without credible information are abuses of law.
legal_principles.held: This again is a blatant abuse of law.

legal_principles.principle: Threats and physical violence by a person in Authority, including a police officer, can cause grave mental torture.
legal_principles.held: When the threats proceed from a person in Authority and that too by a police officer the mental torture caused by it is even more grave.

legal_principles.principle: Police officers must not use their authority to intimidate or coerce individuals into making statements.
legal_principles.held: It is difficult to understand why Sukhpal Singh SSI assaulted Nidhi on her leg with danda and poked it in her stomach. Where was the need to threaten her?

legal_principles.held: Adultery is the sexual intercourse of two persons, either of whom is married to a third person. This clearly supposes the subsistence of marriage between the husband and wife and if during the subsistence of marriage, the wife lives in adultery, she cannot claim Maintenance Allowance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

legal_principles.principle: A wife is not entitled to Maintenance Allowance from her husband if she has refused to live with him without any sufficient reason.

legal_principles.held: Under this provision, a wife is not entitled to any Maintenance Allowance from her husband if she is living in adultery or if she has refused to live with her husband without any sufficient reason or if they are living separately by mutual consent.

outcome.final_order: The wife is entitled to receive maintenance for a period of seven months.

legal_principles.significance: MEDIUM — applies to divorce cases involving ex parte decrees

legal_principles.principle: A Hindu marriage must be performed with the requisite ceremonies in accordance with applicable customs or usage.
legal_principles.held: Therefore, requisite ceremonies for the solemnisation of the Hindu marriage must be in accordance with the applicable customs or usage and where saptapadi has been adopted, the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

legal_principles.principle: A mere issuance of a certificate by an entity in the absence of the requisite ceremonies having been performed does not confirm any marital status to the parties nor establish a marriage under Hindu law.
legal_principles.held: Unless the parties have undergone such ceremony, there would be no Hindu marriage according to Section 7 of the Act and a mere issuance of a certificate by an entity in the absence of the requisite ceremonies having been performed, would neither confirm any marital status to the parties nor establish a marriage under Hindu law.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 2017 and have a minor child born in 2018. The wife filed this petition to transfer the divorce case from the trial court to the Sub Court at Poonamallee.

legal_principles.principle: Parents are duty bound to maintain their minor children.
legal_principles.held: Such an approach of the respondent, who is a Public Servant, at no circumstances, be encouraged by this Court.

legal_principles.principle: For grant of Interim Maintenance to the minor children, no application is required.
legal_principles.held: Even in the absence of any application, the Courts are bound to consider grant of Interim Maintenance in the interest of the minor children and to protect their livelihood, which is the Fundamental Right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

legal_principles.principle: Remedy of maintenance is the measure of social justice as envisaged under the Constitution to prevent the wife and the children from falling into destitution and vagrancy.
legal_principles.held: Preamble and Article 39 and 15(3) of the Indian Constitution envisage social justice and positive State action for empowerment of women and children.

legal_principles.principle: Courts must act as a custodian of minor children when such children are neglected by either of the parents.
legal_principles.held: When the mother of the child is unemployed and living along with her parents mostly is the situation prevailing in our country. Grandparents are burdened with the minor children and the fathers are attempting to escape from the clutches of liability, which cannot be tolerated by the Courts.

legal_principles.principle: The father being the natural guardian under the Guardian and Wards Act, is bound to maintain his minor daughter or son by paying maintenance even in such circumstances where there is a matrimonial dispute.
legal_principles.held: Such rights are to be established considering various other facts and circumstances. Whether the father or mother is entitled for a visitation is to be considered based on the facts and circumstances of each case and not allowing the father or mother to have visitation right will not be a ground to deny Interim Maintenance to the minor child during the pendency of the matrimonial disputes.

outcome.final_order: The respondent agreed to pay interim maintenance of Rs.5,000/- per month to the minor child and directed to deposit it in the wife's bank account.

outcome.final_order: The trial court's decision was upheld, and Halkai was not liable to pay maintenance to Savitri Bai.

legal_principles.principle: The quashment of FIR's and criminal proceedings can be allowed in exceptional circumstances for furthering the cause of justice, especially in cases where matrimonial disputes involving two families are amicably settled subsequent to registration of the FIR.
legal_principles.held: Notwithstanding, the satisfaction of this Court to allow the instant petition in the backdrop of the settlement between the parties, it is needful to mention that in case the FIR's and the criminal cases culminating from the investigations are allowed to be quashed in a routine manner and at the wish of the complainants and/or accused, the criminal justice system is likely to become a causality and the society at large will have to bear the consequences.

legal_principles.principle: The powers of the court under Section 528 of Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita to quash FIR's and criminal proceedings are not restricted by the provisions of Section 345 of the Code corresponding to Section 320 of the Central Code (both repealed) and corresponding to Section 359 of the BNSS.
legal_principles.held: The provisions of the Section 320 of the Code of 1973 corresponding to the Section 359 of the new Code i.e. Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 do not restrict but limit and circumvent the powers of this Court under Section 482 of the Code corresponding to Section 528 of the BNSS regarding quashment of FIR's and criminal proceedings, for the sake of the society at large, which is the real beneficiary of the criminal justice delivery system.
cited_cases: Gopakumar B. Nair Vs. CBI; (2014) 5 SCC 800

outcome.final_order: FIR quashed as parties have compromised their matrimonial dispute and decided to dissolve their marriage.

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty can be established by a pattern of behaviour that causes mental and emotional distress.
legal_principles.held: She deprived the respondent of showering his love and affection towards the child which caused him immense pain, agony and trauma.

legal_principles.principle: A pattern of behaviour that causes mental and emotional distress can be considered as cruelty.
legal_principles.held: She continued to subvert her behaviour believing that birth of child would improve her behaviour but nothing changed despite even thereafter.

legal_principles.principle: A party's failure to meet their obligations can be considered as cruelty.
legal_principles.held: He was given to understand that at the time of marriage the father of appellant had expired, but he subsequently came to know that the father was alive at the time of solemnization of marriage.

outcome.final_order: Divorce granted on grounds of desertion under Section 13 (1)(ib) of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

legal_principles.principle: Courts ought to consider the ground of desertion when it is admitted between parties during the course of trial.

judgments.facts_of_case: A woman married a man when the earlier marriage had not been dissolved in accordance with law and the first wife was still living. She claimed maintenance under Section 18 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.

legal_principles.principle: A person's claim of maintenance will accrue only if the second marriage was a valid one.
legal_principles.held: It was held that the first wife's claim of maintenance will accrue only if the second marriage was a valid one.
cited_cases: Saraswathamma Vs. Bhadramma (AIR 1970 Mysore 157)

legal_principles.principle: A woman can be given recognition either as the wife of a man or as his concubine, but there cannot be an intermediary clause.
legal_principles.held: It was held that in law, a woman can be given recognition either as the wife of a man or as his concubine and that there cannot be an intermediary clause picturesquely described as an 'illegitimate wife'.
cited_cases: A.P.K. Narayanaswamy Reddiar V. Padmanabhan (minor) and others (1966 (1) MLJ 529)

legal_principles.principle: The expression 'wife' in Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure means a legally wedded wife.
legal_principles.held: It was held that the expression 'wife' in Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure means a legally wedded wife.
cited_cases: Smt. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav V. Anantrao Shivram Adhav and another

legal_principles.principle: A bigamous marriage is void ipso jure, that is, void from the very inception.
legal_principles.held: It was held that in marriage of a woman with a man already having a living spouse as per Hindu rites is a complete nullity. The Supreme Court considered the provisions of Sections 11 and 12 of Hindu Marriage Act and held that while the cases covered by Section 12 are not void ab initio and such marriages continue to be effective unless the aggrieved party chooses to avoid it.
cited_cases: Smt. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav V. Anantrao Shivram Adhav and another

outcome.final_order: The court held that a woman who marries a man when the earlier marriage has not been dissolved in accordance with law and the first wife is still living, is entitled to claim maintenance under Section 18 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.

legal_principles.principle: Either party to a marriage has the right to present a petition for dissolution of the marriage on the ground that there has been no restitution of conjugal rights between the parties for a period of one year after the passing of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights.
legal_principles.held: A perusal of the above makes it clear that either party to a marriage whether solemnised before or after the commencement of the Act has a right to present a petition for the dissolution of a marriage on the ground that there has been no restitution of conjugal rights between the parties to the marriage for a period of one year after the passing of the decree for restitution of conjugal rights.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party alleging desertion to prove it.
legal_principles.held: According to the Family Court, the allegation of desertion made by the petitioner has not been proved.

outcome.final_order: Family Court's decision to dismiss the petition is set aside. A decree of divorce may be granted under Section 13(1A)(ii) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner and respondent got married in March 2017 but separated just a month later. They have no children. The parties entered into a settlement, returning dowry articles and settling alimony. Petitioner seeks waiver of the six-month statutory period for granting divorce.

legal_principles.principle: The period mentioned in Section 13-B (2) of the Hindu Marriage Act is directory and not mandatory.
legal_principles.held: The Hon'ble Apex Court has observed that the period mentioned in Section 13-B (2) of Hindu Marriage Act is not mandatory, rather the same is directory and it is open to the Court to exercise its discretion in the facts and circumstances of the case.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh vs Harveen Kaur, (2017) 4 RCR (Civil) 608

legal_principles.principle: The Court has to consider the period for which the parties have been married, duration of their separation, duration of pending litigation and any other pending litigation between them.
legal_principles.held: The Court has to see whether there is any possibility of parties resuming cohabitation or chances of alternative rehabilitation for the purpose of waiving the statutory period of six months.

legal_principles.principle: The discretion to waive the period is a guided discretion by considering the interest of justice where there is no chance of reconciliation and parties were already separated for a longer period or contesting the proceedings for a period longer than the period mentioned in Section 13-B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.
legal_principles.held: The Court has to consider the period for which the parties have been married, duration of their separation, duration of pending litigation and any other pending litigation between them.

outcome.final_order: The court waived the statutory period of six months and granted divorce to the parties.

judgments.case_name: Kaithakulangara Kunhikannan vs Nellatham Veettil Malu
judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner, a Hindu husband, sought judicial separation from his wife under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act. The trial court granted judicial separation and ordered maintenance to the respondent at Rs. 25/- per mensem.

legal_principles.principle: A wife who has been living in adultery is not entitled to maintenance under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, unless there are very special grounds.
legal_principles.held: In our opinion, such a meeting place of law and morality is Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, or for the matter of that Section 18 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act. In the exercise of judicial discretion, expressly vested in Courts of Law under Section 25 (1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, a Judge should, unless there be very special grounds, leave a wife divorced on the ground of proved unchastity or adultery, to the resources of her immorality and deny her the lawful means of support, by passing a decree for maintenance in her favour.
cited_cases: Sachindra Nath v. Banamala, AIR 1960 Cal 575
Amar Kanta v. Soyana, AIR 1960 Cal 438

legal_principles.principle: A finding of unchastity recorded during judicial separation proceedings regarding the wife's unchastity must and should be taken into account when an order is being passed under Section 25 (1) of the Hindu Marriage Act.
legal_principles.held: In my opinion, if a subsequent conduct of the wife who has become unchaste can form the basis for cancellation of an order passed under Setton 25 (1), a finding recorded during the judicial separation proceedings regarding the unchastity of the wife must and should be taken into account even in the first instance, when an order is being passed under Section 25 (1) of the Act.
cited_cases: Vaidialingam, J. posed the question in the following manner: 'Where a charge of adultery is the very foundation of a claim for asking judicial separation and that claim is accepted by a court notwithstanding that finding the respondent against whom that finding has been entered, can claim, as of right, to be awarded maintenance under Section 25 of the Act'
use_in: cases involving judicial separation and adultery

outcome.final_order: The final order was that the respondent is entitled only to bare maintenance allowance, payable monthly from the date of the order.

judgments.case_name: K.Mirdula vs Sakthi Raj
judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner and respondent were married in 2019. They have a one-and-a-half-year-old daughter. The petitioner is unemployed and seeking maintenance to care for the child.

legal_principles.principle: Courts are bound to protect the interest of minor children at all circumstances.
legal_principles.held: However, the interest of the minor child is of paramount importance and the Courts are bound to protect the interest of the minor children at all circumstances.

legal_principles.principle: Remedy of maintenance is a social justice as envisaged under the Constitution to prevent the child from falling into destitution or vagrant.
legal_principles.held: Remedy of maintenance is a social justice as envisaged under the Constitution to prevent the child from falling into destitution or vagrant.

legal_principles.principle: Courts are bound to consider the grant of interim maintenance even in the absence of any application from the mother till such time the final maintenance is to be determined after adjudication.
legal_principles.held: Thus, the Family Courts or the Courts dealing with the matrimonial cases are bound to consider the grant of interim maintenance even in the absence of any application from the mother till such time the final maintenance is to be determined after adjudication.

legal_principles.principle: The Courts are directed to look into the issues and consider for grant of interim maintenance to protect the livelihood of the children residing with the unemployed mother.
legal_principles.held: In all such cases, the Courts are directed to look into the issues and consider for grant of interim maintenance to protect the livelihood of the children residing with the unemployed mother.

outcome.final_order: Interim maintenance was ordered by the court to protect the livelihood of the minor child.

legal_principles.held: It is settled law that the court cannot waive the cooling period unless there are exceptional circumstances which justify such a waiver. The burden lies on the applicant to establish that there are such exceptional circumstances.

legal_principles.principle: The court cannot waive the cooling period unless there are exceptional circumstances which justify such a waiver.
legal_principles.held: It is settled law that the court cannot waive the cooling period unless there are exceptional circumstances which justify such a waiver.

judgments.facts_of_case: The respondent filed a case against the petitioner and 8 others for alleged offence under Section 494 r/w 109 I.P.C. The petitioner was convicted and sentenced. He then appealed to this court.

legal_principles.principle: At the appellate stage, a party cannot adduce additional evidence as a matter of fact.
legal_principles.held: The learned judge observed that at that time, the petitioner had not raised any questions with regard to the evidence let in by P.W.1 in C.C.No.426 of 2004.

legal_principles.principle: A party cannot say that only now they have come to know about the evidence let in by a witness, if the evidence was recorded in their presence.
legal_principles.held: The learned judge observed that P.W.1 was examined in chief in C.C.No.426 of 2004, on 21.07.2005 itself.

legal_principles.principle: A party cannot recall a witness for cross-examination after the main case has been decided on merits.
legal_principles.held: The learned judge observed that at this stage, the petition was filed before the trial Court for additional evidence in order to drag on the proceedings.

legal_principles.principle: A party cannot delay the proceedings by filing multiple petitions.
legal_principles.held: The learned counsel for the respondent argued that the revision petitioner had filed one more Criminal Revision before this Court for transfer of the appeal. That was however dismissed.

outcome.final_order: The trial court's order is set aside.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 1984. The husband filed for divorce citing cruelty and desertion. The wife refused to live with the husband after 1986 and left him with their children. The trial court granted a decree for dissolution of marriage.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse who refuses to live with the other and takes their children away is considered deserted.
legal_principles.held: The trial Court found that the appellant/wife was living with the respondent/husband till the year 1986. She lived with the respondent/husband only for about 3 years and thereafter, she refused to live with the respondent/husband.

legal_principles.principle: A party's refusal to live with the other and taking children away can be considered desertion.
legal_principles.held: The trial Court arrived a conclusion that the appellant/wife deserted the respondent/husband and therefore, he is entitled for the relief of dissolution of marriage.

outcome.final_order: The appeal was allowed, and the decree for dissolution of marriage was set aside.

judgments.facts_of_case: The appellant filed a suit to declare herself as the single unmarried mother. The Family Court held that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit since there was no marital relationship between the parties. Aggrieved by this decision, the appellant appealed.

legal_principles.principle: A Family Court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit for declaration that the appellant is the single unmarried mother.
legal_principles.held: The suit or petition for declaration as single unmarried mother is squarely covered under Section 7(e) of the Family Courts Act and, thus, the Family Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit.

legal_principles.principle: A Family Court may not entertain a suit for declaratory relief if it does not have jurisdiction.
legal_principles.held: The Family Court has not entertained the suit of the appellant, as it has no jurisdiction.

outcome.final_order: The appeal is allowed.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties got married in 2007. A child was born out of wedlock in 2008. The wife filed an application under Section 125 Cr.P.C. seeking maintenance from the husband. The trial court granted interim maintenance, which was later reduced.

legal_principles.principle: Courts are not only guided by the income of the husband in determining the amount of monthly maintenance.
legal_principles.held: While awarding maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C. or maintenance pendente lite under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act or the maintenance under Section 18 of the Hindu Adoption or Maintenance Act, Courts are not only guided by the income of the husband in determining the amount of monthly maintenance.

legal_principles.principle: Several factors including the status of the parties, liabilities, if any, of the husband and number of persons to be maintained by the husband would be some of the factors to be taken into consideration.
legal_principles.held: The Higher Courts have held that several factors including the status of the parties, liabilities, if any, of the husband and number of persons to be maintained by the husband would be some of the factors to be taken into consideration.
cited_cases: Alok Kumar Jain v. Purnima Jain, (2007) DRJ 115
Lalit Bhola vs Nidhi Bhola & Anr., (2013) X SCC Y

legal_principles.principle: The amount required by the wife to live a similar life style as she enjoyed in the matrimonial home keeping in view food, clothing, shelter, educational and medical needs of the wife and the children, if any, residing with the wife and payment capacity of the husband.
legal_principles.held: The amount required by the wife to live a similar life style as she enjoyed in the matrimonial home keeping in view food, clothing, shelter, educational and medical needs of the wife and the children, if any, residing with the wife and payment capacity of the husband.
cited_cases: Lalit Bhola vs Nidhi Bhola & Anr., (2013) X SCC Y

legal_principles.principle: There cannot be any mathematical formula for award of the maintenance amount such as 1/3rd or any other proportion of the husband's income.

judgments.case_name: Laxmibai Nagappa Matiwadar And Ors. vs Limbabai Nagappa Matiwadar

parties.petitioner_plaintiff: Laxmibai Nagappa Matiwadar and others (wife, husband's relatives)

judgments.facts_of_case: Suit filed by respondent for possession of three plots relying on her right to succeed to the interest of her husband Nagappa. Appellants' marriage was void, and children born from this marriage were illegitimate.

legal_principles.principle: Legitimacy under section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act confers status on children born out of void and voidable marriages.
legal_principles.held: The Joint Committee's report clearly indicates that in no case, the off-springs of void or voidable marriage be regarded as illegitimate.

legal_principles.principle: The express declaration in section 16(1) of the Act takes away and eclipses the general rule that the off-spring of a marriage, which is null and void ipso jure, is illegitimate.
legal_principles.held: Though because of the statue the marriage would be void, that would not lead to the inevitable result of bastardising the children who are born out of such a void wedlock.

legal_principles.principle: The legitimacy conferred by section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act recognises rights in or to the property of parents.
legal_principles.held: Section 16 thus enacts a complete Code with regard to the off-springs of void or voidable marriages. Firstly, it declares the status of such a child being one as legitimate. Secondly, it recognises rights in the property of the parents.

outcome.final_order: Suit decreed with regard to Plot No. 228, holding that appellants would not have any right or interest therein because appellant No. 1 Laxmibai's marriage was void.

judgments.case_name: Lila Gupta vs Laxmi Narain & Ors
judgments.facts_of_case: The husband of the appellant-late Rajendra Kumar had earlier contracted a marriage with one Sarla Gupta. Both Rajendra Kumar and Sarla Gupta filed suits against each other, which were decreed on April 8, 1963 granting divorce. The marriage with the appellant Lila Gupta was solemnised on May 25, 1963. Disputes arose in consolidation proceedings between the appellant claiming as widow of Rajendra Kumar and respondents about succession to Bhumidari rights.

legal_principles.principle: A marriage solemnised before the expiry of the period of limitation for presenting an appeal or where an appeal has been presented, during the pendency of the appeal must be regarded as a void marriage.
legal_principles.held: The English Law and the decisions of the Australian High Court and Indian High Courts which involved the application of s. 57 Indian Divorce Act indicate that a marriage solemnised before the expiry of the period of limitation for presenting an appeal or where an appeal has been presented, during the pendency of the appeal must be regarded as a void marriage.
cited_cases: Chichester v. Mure (falsely called Chichester) (1863) 3, SW. & Tr., 223
Warter v. Warter, (1890) 15 P., 152

legal_principles.principle: A contention that a marriage solemnised in violation of the main provision of s. 15 is a nullity cannot be summarily rejected.
legal_principles.held: At the lowest, there is good ground for saying that a contention that a marriage solemnised in violation of the main provision of s. 15 is a nullity cannot be summarily rejected.
cited_cases: Chichester v. Mure (falsely called Chichester) (1863) 3, SW. & Tr., 223
Warter v. Warter, (1890) 15 P., 152

outcome.final_order: The Court held that the marriage contracted by Rajendra Kumar with Lila Gupta was not void, but merely invalid. The parties were subject to a binding tie of wedlock flowing from the marriage.

judgments.case_name: Lingla Nirupama Reddy vs Lingala Venkata Narasimha Reddy
judgments.facts_of_case: The Petitioner filed a petition for divorce against the Respondent under Section 13(1) (ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The marriage was consummated but no children were born out of the wedlock. The Respondent tortured the Petitioner over petty issues and demanded additional dowry.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party alleging cruelty to prove the same.
legal_principles.held: The petitioner voluntarily withdrew from the company of the respondent, without any justifiable cause and consistently refused to resume cohabitation despite repeated requests and efforts for reconciliation.

legal_principles.principle: A party's refusal to resume cohabitation despite efforts for reconciliation can be a factor in determining the existence of cruelty.
legal_principles.held: The respondent stated to have made sincere attempts for mediation and reunion, whereas the petitioner remained adamant in refusing conjugal companionship.

legal_principles.principle: The absence of a criminal complaint during the subsistence of marriage can indicate that no cruelty occurred.
legal_principles.held: The non-filing of any criminal complaint by the petitioner during the subsistence of marriage, categorically indicates that no cruelty, as alleged, ever occurred.

outcome.result: Appeal disposed of by this common Judgment
outcome.final_order: The petition filed by the Petitioner seeking divorce was dismissed, and the counter claim preferred by the Respondent seeking restitution of conjugal rights was also dismissed.

legal_principles.principle: The respondent may claim any relief available to him under the Act in a proceeding instituted by one spouse.
legal_principles.held: Under section 23-A of the Act, in a proceeding instituted by one spouse the other spouse as respondent can claim any of the reliefs available to him under the Act.

legal_principles.principle: The Court may give to the respondent any relief under this Act if the petitioner's adultery, cruelty or desertion is proved.
legal_principles.held: If the petitioner's adultery, cruelty or desertion is proved, the Court may give to the respondent any relief under this Act to which he or she would have been entitled if he or she had presented any petition seeking such relief on that ground.

legal_principles.principle: The Court can fix interim maintenance for payment to the one spouse by other where one of them is unable to maintain him or her and the other has means to do so.
legal_principles.held: Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the Court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the Court to be reasonable.

legal_principles.principle: A decree for dissolution of marriage can be granted only on the grounds specified in the Indian Divorce Act.
legal_principles.held: The ground on which a husband may obtain a decree for dissolution of marriage is the adultery of the wife. legal_principles.principle: A decree for judicial separation can be granted on the ground of cruelty.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner married respondent in 1964, but they separated. Petitioner later married again. Respondent claimed maintenance from petitioner due to his second marriage.

legal_principles.principle: A wife is entitled to be maintained with dignity of a wife and as Justice Fazl Ali said, the salutory provisions of the Code are not merely meant to provide a wife with food, clothing and lodging as if she is only a chattel.
legal_principles.held: The immortal bird of India. Kalidass brought out through the lips of king Aja in Raghubansam the concept of a wife as 'GRUHINI SACHIBA SAKHl MITTHAH, PRIYA SHISYA......', i.e. that the wife is a partner to the husband and is his advisor, his friend and his dearest disciple

legal_principles.principle: The right of the wife to refuse to live with the husband in case of his second marriage is not confined to the offer of the husband to maintain her only after an order Under Section 125(1), Cr PC has been passed.
legal_principles.held: Indeed there is no reason as to why a distinction should be maintained between a wife who desires to file a petition to claim maintenance on the ground of the husband's second marriage and the wife whose husband has contracted a second marriage after an order of maintenance has been passed and makes an offer to maintain the wife but she refuses to live with him in view of a second marriage.

XXXVII (1971) CLT 954

outcome.final_order: Maintenance of Rs. 300/- per month to the opposite party No. 1 and Rs. 200/- per month to the opp party No. 2, the daughter through her, was granted.

legal_principles.principle: A person who is ready to take back his wife and resume their conjugal life in terms of the decree for restitution of conjugal rights cannot seek to avoid payment of maintenance as ordered by the trial Court.
legal_principles.held: After recording the evidence of both the parties and on proper appreciation of the same, the learned Judge came to the conclusion that the petitioner herein has discarded the 1st respondent herein, who is his wife and neglected her and that he is not providing anything towards her maintenance.

legal_principles.principle: A person who is not providing anything towards his wife's maintenance cannot seek to avoid payment of maintenance as ordered by the trial Court.
legal_principles.held: So, in view of the said finding recorded by the learned Judge on proper appreciation of evidence on record, the petitioner now cannot seek to avoid payment of maintenance as ordered by the trial Court on the ground that he is now ready and willing to take back his wife and resume their conjugal life in terms of the decree for restitution of conjugal rights.

outcome.final_order: The final order confirmed the trial court's decision granting maintenance of Rs.5,500/- per month to the respondent.

legal_principles.principle: The power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code is to be exercised sparingly and with caution.
legal_principles.held: No doubt, under Section 482 of the Code, the High Court has inherent power to quash the criminal proceedings even in those cases which are not compoundable, where the parties have settled the matter between themselves.

legal_principles.principle: The guiding factor in quashing criminal proceedings is to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of the process of any Court.
legal_principles.held: When the parties have reached the settlement and on that basis petition for quashing the criminal proceedings is filed, the guiding factor in such cases would be to secure: (i) ends of justice, or (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court.

legal_principles.principle: Criminal cases involving heinous and serious offences, such as murder, rape, or dacoity, should not be quashed merely on the basis of a settlement between the parties.
legal_principles.held: Such offences are not private in nature and have a serious impact on society. Similarly, for offences alleged to have been committed under special statute like the Prevention of Corruption Act or the offences committed by Public Servants while working in that capacity are not to be quashed merely on the basis of compromise between the victim and the offender.

legal_principles.principle: Criminal cases having overwhelmingly and predominantly civil character, particularly those arising out of commercial transactions or family disputes, should be quashed when the parties have resolved their entire disputes among themselves.
legal_principles.held: On the other, those criminal cases having overwhelmingly and pre-dominantly civil character, particularly those arising out of commercial transactions or arising out of matrimonial relationship or family disputes should be quashed when the parties have resolved their entire disputes among themselves.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner is the wife of respondent and seeks withdrawal of divorce proceedings in F.C.O.P.No. 158/2023 and transfer to another court.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party seeking transfer of a case to establish sufficient reasons for such transfer.
legal_principles.held: The material on record prima facie goes to show that, due to the matrimonial disputes between both the spouses, the petitioner/wife has been residing separately along with her child aged about 5 years in Machilipatnam and she filed (03) cases against the respondent/husband herein i.e., C.C.No.424 of 2023 on the file of the Special Judicial Magistrate of First Class (Prohibition & Excise) Court, Machilipatnam, P.R.C.No.22 of 2023 and Maintenance Case vide M.C.No.39 of 2023 on the file of the II Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Machilipatnam, Krishna District, the aforesaid cases are pending for adjudication.

legal_principles.principle: A party's convenience or inconvenience is not a sufficient reason to transfer a case.
legal_principles.held: Learned counsel for the petitioner would further contend that the petitioner being a woman, has been residing separately along with her child aged about 5 years and depending upon the mercy of her parents at Machilipatnam and the distance between Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam is more than 360Kms, it is very difficult for her to travel to attend the divorce case proceedings which was filed by the respondent/husband, before the Court at Visakhapatnam without any male assistance.

outcome.final_order: The High Court may be pleased to pass orders by withdrawing the Divorce O.P., in F.C.O.P.No. 158/2023 on the file of the Court of the Judge Family Court-cum-V Additional District Judge at Visakhapatnam and same may be transferred to the Court of the Principal Civil Judge (Senior Division), Machilipatnam, Krishna District.

judgments.facts_of_case: Appellant filed divorce petition under Section 13 of Hindu Marriage Act. Trial court dismissed the petition. Appellant appealed and also applied for maintenance pendente lite and litigation expenses.

legal_principles.principle: The defence is to be struck off if the order passed under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act for the grant of maintenance pendente lite is not complied with.
legal_principles.held: I he effect of non-compliance of the order passed on the application under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act for the grant of maintenance pendente lite is that the defence is to be struck off.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse is liable to pay litigation expenses and maintenance allowance throughout the litigation proceedings if an application is filed under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act.
legal_principles.held: In view of the clear provision contained in the Act, I am of the firm view that the husband is liable to pay litigation expenses and maintenance allowance throughout the litigation proceedings.

outcome.final_order: Husband's defence struck off due to non-compliance with court order regarding payment of maintenance pendente lite and litigation expenses.

judgments.case_name: Paras Ram vs Janki Bai
judgments.facts_of_case: A petition under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 was filed by Paras Ram against Janki Bai. An application for relief under Section 24 of the Act was made before the learned Civil Judge by Janki Bai and he passed an order to stay further proceedings on the petition until Paras Ram paid Rs. 250/- to Janki Bai as ordered.

legal_principles.principle: An appeal from an order of a civil judge passed in a proceeding under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act lies to the District Judge if a certain condition is fulfilled and to the High Court if it is not.
legal_principles.held: The residuary power is thus vested in the High Court and an appeal lies to the District Judge only if the condition is fulfilled.

legal_principles.principle: When no value was fixed on the petition and when there is no law also under which a certain value or a value not below or not exceeding a certain sum ought to have been fixed, it cannot be said that the value of the petition did not exceed Rs. 10,000/-.
legal_principles.held: When no value was fixed on the petition and when there was no law also under which a certain value or a value not below or not exceeding a certain sum ought to have been fixed, it cannot be said that the value of the petition did not exceed Rs. 10,000/-.
applicable_acts_sections: Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Courts Act, 1887 — Section 21
cited_cases: Paras Ram vs Janki Bai, (1961) X SCC Y

outcome.final_order: The question of whether the appeal lies to this Court or to the Court of the District Judge, Kanpur was decided in favor of the appellant.

judgments.case_name: P.Geetha vs V.Kirubaharan
judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 2020 and have a 11-month-old child. The husband filed for dissolution of marriage, but the wife is unable to travel from Tiruchirappalli to contest the case. She also seeks interim maintenance for her child.

legal_principles.principle: Parents are duty bound to maintain their minor children.
legal_principles.held: The 11 months old female child has to be taken care of by the father, who is the natural guardian and an earning member.

legal_principles.principle: The Courts are bound to consider grant of Interim Maintenance in the interest of the minor children and to protect their livelihood.
legal_principles.held: For grant of Interim Maintenance to the minor children, no application is required. Even in the absence of any application, the Courts are bound to consider grant of Interim Maintenance in the interest of the minor children and to protect their livelihood, which is the Fundamental Right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

legal_principles.principle: Maintenance is dependent upon factual situations; the Court should mould the claim for maintenance based on various factors brought before it.
legal_principles.held: Maintenance is dependent upon factual situations; the Court should mould the claim for maintenance based on various factors brought before it. The courts have held that if the wife is earning, it cannot operate as a bar from being awarded maintenance by the husband.

legal_principles.principle: The obligation of the husband to provide maintenance stands on a higher pedestal than the wife.
legal_principles.held: The obligation of the husband to provide maintenance stands on a higher pedestal than the wife.

outcome.final_order: The respondent was directed to pay a sum of Rs.5,000/- towards Interim Maintenance to be paid to the petitioner for the purpose of maintenance of the minor child.

judgments.facts_of_case: The husband filed for divorce and the wife remained ex parte. The court passed an ex parte decree in favour of the husband. The wife then sought to condone a delay in filing an application to set aside the decree.

legal_principles.principle: Remarriage of the petitioner cannot be a reason to dismiss an application filed by the respondent for setting aside an ex parte decree.
legal_principles.held: Therefore, there is no legality or perversity in the order passed by the trial Court setting aside the ex parte decree of divorce passed against the respondent / wife after condoning the delay of 53 days in filing an application and prays for dismissing this Civil Revision Petition.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the respondent to provide a proper explanation for condoning the delay in filing an application to set aside an ex parte decree.

outcome.final_order: The Civil Revision Petition is preferred against the order dated 19.03.2024 made in I.A.No.100 of 2022 in HMOP.No.33 of 2020.

legal_principles.significance: HIGH — highlights the importance of a minor's actions in determining whether an accused has taken them away from their lawful guardian

outcome.final_order: No offence punishable under Section 363 of IPC will be made out when the girl is aged more than 16 years and is mature enough to understand what she is doing.

The trial court returned the plaint to the Petitioner-Appellant on the ground of lack of territorial jurisdiction.

legal_principles.principle: The court where the parties last resided together or the marriage was solemnized has jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Section 9 or other provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act.
legal_principles.held: So as per the contingencies prescribed above under Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act, the court where the parties last resided together or the marriage was solemnized has also the jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Section 9 or other provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act.

legal_principles.principle: A petition under the Hindu Marriage Act must be presented to the district court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction—marriage was solemnized, respondent resides, parties last resided together, or petitioner is residing.
legal_principles.held: Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act speaks as follows: '19. Court to which petition shall be presented.—Every petition under this Act shall be presented to the district Court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction—(i) the marriage was solemnized, or (ii) the respondent, at the time of the presentation of the petition, resides, or (iii) the parties to the marriage last resided together, or [(iii-a) in case of the wife is the petitioner, where she is residing on the date of presentation of the petition, or] (iv) the petitioner is residing at the time of the presentation of the petition, in a case where the respondent is, at that time, residing outside the territories to which this Act extends, or has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven years or more by those persons who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive.'

outcome.final_order: The appeal is allowed.

legal_principles.held: Counsel further submitted that by virtue of Section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872 the Courts have ample powers to compare the admitted writings and signatures with the disputed signatures and handwritings of any party to the suit or witness and while doing so, the court can also take the help of any other corroborative evidence including the opinion of handwriting expert and then form its own opinion.

judgments.case_name: Shamsher Singh vs Sunita Jamwal
judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioners seek waiver of six months for recording second motion under Section 13-B of Hindu Marriage Act.

legal_principles.principle: The discretion to waive the statutory period is guided by considering the interest of justice.
legal_principles.held: The discretion to waive the period is a guided discretion by considering the interest of justice where there is no chance of reconciliation and parties were already separated for a longer period or contesting proceedings for a period longer than the period mentioned in Section 13-B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

legal_principles.principle: The Court has to consider the period for which the parties have been married, duration of their separation, duration of pending litigation and any other pending litigation between them.
legal_principles.held: The Court has to consider the period for which the parties have been married, duration of their separation, duration of pending litigation and any other pending litigation between them.

legal_principles.principle: The compromise arrived at between the parties has to be genuine in nature and the same should take care of alimony, custody of child (if any) and any other issues between them.
legal_principles.held: The compromise arrived at between the parties has to be genuine in nature and the same should take care of alimony, custody of child (if any) and any other issues between them.

legal_principles.principle: The Court has to be satisfied that the parties are living separately for more than the statutory period and all efforts at Mediation and Conciliation Centre have been tried and have failed.
legal_principles.held: The Court has to be satisfied that the parties are living separately for more than the statutory period and all efforts at Mediation and Conciliation Centre have been tried and have failed and there is no chance of reconciliation and further waiting period will only add to the agony of the parties.

legal_principles.principle: The waiting period will only prolong their agony.
legal_principles.held: The waiting period will only prolong their agony.

outcome.final_order: Court waived the period of six months for recording second motion.

legal_principles.principle: The power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code is to be exercised sparingly and with caution.
legal_principles.held: No doubt, under Section 482 of the Code, the High Court has inherent power to quash the criminal proceedings even in those cases which are not compoundable, where the parties have settled the matter between themselves.

legal_principles.principle: The guiding factor in quashing criminal proceedings is to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of the process of any Court.
legal_principles.held: When the parties have reached the settlement and on that basis petition for quashing the criminal proceedings is filed, the guiding factor in such cases would be to secure: (i) ends of justice, or (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court.

legal_principles.principle: Criminal cases involving heinous and serious offences, such as murder, rape, or dacoity, should not be quashed merely on the basis of a settlement between the parties.
legal_principles.held: Such offences are not private in nature and have a serious impact on society. Similarly, for offences alleged to have been committed under special statute like the Prevention of Corruption Act or the offences committed by Public Servants while working in that capacity are not to be quashed merely on the basis of compromise between the victim and the offender.

legal_principles.principle: Criminal cases having overwhelmingly and predominantly civil character, particularly those arising out of commercial transactions or family disputes, should be quashed when the parties have resolved their entire disputes among themselves.
legal_principles.held: On the other, those criminal cases having overwhelmingly and pre−dominantly civil character, particularly those arising out of commercial transactions or arising out of matrimonial relationship or family disputes should be quashed when the parties have resolved their entire disputes among themselves.

outcome.final_order: FIR No. 181/15, dated 8.9.2015, under Sections 498−A, 406, 323, 504 and 34 of IPC, is quashed.

legal_principles.held: To prove the domestic relationship the petitioner is required to prove that she and the respondent have lived together in a relationship of marriage or in a relationship in the nature of marriage or related by consanguinity or adoption or as family members living together as a joint family.

legal_principles.principle: To prove domestic violence under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the petitioner must establish that the respondent has subjected her to acts of domestic violence as contemplated under section 3 of the Act.
legal_principles.held: To prove the act of domestic violence the petitioner is required to prove any one or more of the acts committed by the respondent as contemplated under section 3 of the Act.
applicable_acts_sections: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Section 3
keywords: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

outcome.final_order: The petition was filed under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and the court granted the relief sought by the petitioner.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner and respondent filed a petition under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The trial court fixed the matter for mediation and directed the parties to appear on 22.04.2026. The petitioner moved an application seeking waiver of the cooling period.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party seeking waiver of cooling period to establish justifiable grounds.
legal_principles.held: The contention that one of the parties had already resolved to re-marry fixing 15.04.2026 as the date of marriage without seeking divorce, in itself is not a valid ground and it cannot also give rise to any justifiable ground for waiving of the cooling of period.
cited_cases: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur; (2017) (8) SCC 746

legal_principles.principle: The court will not waive the cooling period unless there are justifiable grounds.
legal_principles.held: There was no urgency in the matter and since the mediation was already fixed on 22.04.2026, hence, there was no justifiable ground to waive of the cooling period.

outcome.final_order: The High Court directed the Additional Principal Judge, Family Court No. 7, Lucknow to expedite the hearing of the petition.

judgments.case_name: Smt. Meera vs Vijay Shankar Talchidia
judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 1976, but no child was born. The husband sought divorce alleging cruelty and adultery. The wife denied the allegations.

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty as a ground of divorce under Section 13(1)(ia) is a conduct of such type that the petitioner could not reasonably be expected to live with the respondent.
legal_principles.held: Now, the act or omission or conduct which constitutes cruelty need not cause any sort of apprehension in the mind of the petitioner.

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty is a conduct of such type that the relations between the parties had deteriorated to such an extent due to the conduct of one of the spouses that it has become impossible for them to live together without mental agony, torture or distress.
legal_principles.held: It has not been defined in the Act as it was not possible to do so. Section 13(1)(ia) has undergone a change by 1976 amendment made by the Parliament.

legal_principles.principle: What may amount to cruelty in one case may not amount to cruelty in another case.
legal_principles.held: No rigid meaning can be assigned to cruelty in order to come under Section 13. What may amount to cruelty in one case may not amount to cruelty in another case.

legal_principles.principle: The court dealing with a petition for divorce under Section 13 is expected to bear in mind that the problem before it is that of human beings and that all psychological changes in a man's conduct has to be borne in mind before granting or rejecting the petition.
legal_principles.held: The court dealing with a petition for divorce under Section 13 is expected to bear in mind that the problem before it is that of human beings and that all psychological changes in a man's conduct has to be borne in mind before granting or rejecting the petition.

outcome.final_order: The appeal is allowed.

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty under Section 498-A, IPC means any wilful conduct that is likely to drive a woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health.
legal_principles.held: Explanation (a) provides that 'cruelty' means any wilful conduct, which is of such a nature as, is likely to drive a woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman.

legal_principles.principle: Harassment of a woman under Section 498-A, IPC means coercion to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security.
legal_principles.held: Clause (b) provides that 'cruelty' means harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.

judgments.facts_of_case: Sonu and his wife Premlata are aggrieved by the order dated February 20, 2014 disposing of application filed by Premlata under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. From out of the wedlock a daughter currently aged 9 years and a son currently aged 7 years were born.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse unable to maintain himself/herself is entitled to maintenance on the principle of equi-status and respect that the spouse would have enjoyed if he/she continued to live with other spouse.
legal_principles.held: The object behind Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is to provide for maintenance, pendente-lite, to a spouse in matrimonial proceedings so that during the pendency of the proceedings the spouse can maintain herself/himself and also have sufficient funds to carry on the litigation so that the spouse does not unduly suffer in the conduct of the case for want of funds.

legal_principles.principle: The Court while considering the merits of an application for grant of an interim maintenance under Section 24 has to necessarily arrive at prima-facie determination about the earning capacity of the rival claimants.
legal_principles.held: The Court is called upon to make a summary consideration of amount which the applicant is to be awarded by way of maintenance pendente-lite and litigation expenses in accordance with the financial resources of the parties.

legal_principles.principle: Where there was sufficient means in the family of the husband on the strength of which the husband got married he has to share the burden to support his wife during the course of annulment of such marriage.
legal_principles.held: Where the parties do not come forward with exact income they have, the Court would have no alternative but to apply its guess-work.
cited_cases: 140 (2007) DLT 16 Sh.Bharat Hegde Vs. Smt.Saroj Hegde

outcome.final_order: Premlata has been awarded maintenance in sum of `18,000/- per month from the date of the application filed by Premlata.
