judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner is the legally wedded wife of Late Shri Satanand Mishra, seeking family pension after his death. She claims that second wife is not entitled to get family pension.

legal_principles.principle: A person whose name is mentioned in a nomination form submitted by the deceased government employee is entitled to family pension.
legal_principles.held: Since the name of respondent no.8 is mentioned in nomination form submitted by deceased Govt. employee, therefore, after his death according to nomination done by him, respondent no.8 is entitled for family pension.

legal_principles.principle: A person specified in a nomination under Rule 46 is entitled to receive pension.
legal_principles.held: Rule 45 also lays down that person on whom right to receive is conferred by means of a nomination under Rule 46 is entitled to receive pension.

legal_principles.principle: A person who has not raised any grievance before the answering respondents during the lifetime of the government servant is not entitled to challenge the nomination made by the deceased government employee.
legal_principles.held: Deceased Govt. employee has submitted a nomination under Section 46 of the Pension Rules and has mentioned the name of respondent no.8 in capacity of his wife. Since the name of respondent no.8 is mentioned in nomination form submitted by deceased Govt. employee, therefore, after his death according to nomination done by him, respondent no.8 is entitled for family pension.

legal_principles.principle: A petition involving highly disputed questions and facts is not maintainable and deserves to be dismissed.
legal_principles.held: It is submitted that petition involves highly disputed questions and facts. Facts and issues can only be decided by leading oral and documentary evidence before court of competent jurisdiction.
cited_cases: Smt. Koushalya Bai vs. M.P. State Electricity Board and others, 2006 (1) MPHT 257

judgments.facts_of_case: Rajendra Prasad was the husband of the appellant. He died in a road accident. The respondent is his minor daughter born to his second wife. The appellant stopped maintaining the respondent after her father's death.

legal_principles.principle: A dependant shall be entitled to maintenance from those who take the estate, if they have not obtained a share in the estate by testamentary or intestate succession.
legal_principles.held: The dependant shall be entitled, subject to the provisions of this Act, to maintenance from those who take the estate.
applicable_acts_sections: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 — Section 22

legal_principles.principle: The liability of each person who takes the estate shall be in proportion to the value of the share or part of the estate taken by him or her.
legal_principles.held: The liability of each of the persons who take the estate shall be in proportion to the value of the share or part of the estate taken by him or her.
applicable_acts_sections: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 — Section 22

legal_principles.principle: A person who is himself or herself a dependant shall not be liable to contribute to the maintenance of others, if they have obtained a share or part that would become less than what would be awarded to them by way of maintenance.
legal_principles.held: No person who is himself or herself a dependant shall be liable to contribute to the maintenance of others, if he or she has obtained a share or part, the value of which is, or would, if the liability to contribute were enforced, become less than what would be awarded to him or her by way of maintenance under this Act.
applicable_acts_sections: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 — Section 22

legal_principles.principle: An illegitimate son of a deceased Government servant is entitled to be considered for compassionate appointment.
legal_principles.held: It was held that illegitimate son of the deceased Government servant is also entitled to be considered for compassionate appointment.

legal_principles.principle: A decree for judicial separation under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 can be rescinded if it is considered just and reasonable to do so.

outcome.final_order: The petition for divorce is not maintainable and deserves to be dismissed/rejected.

The said marriage was also registered as required under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. However, at the time when the said marriage was performed, respondent's first wife Lilabai was alive and the said marriage between them was subsisting.

legal_principles.principle: A marriage is null and void if it contravenes the condition under Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
legal_principles.held: Section 11 of the said Act provides that any marriage after the commencement of the Act shall be null and void if it contravened inter alia the said condition under section 5(i).

legal_principles.principle: A marriage between two parties is rendered nugatory if it is null and void under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
legal_principles.held: The consequences of such a marriage being null and void or 'voidipso jure' was that although the marriage was solemnized by performing necessary ceremonies and was registered, the same was in law rendered nugatory as if not having taken place at all.

legal_principles.principle: A woman cannot be considered a legally wedded wife of the man if their marriage is null and void under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
legal_principles.held: Accordingly, in such a case the woman cannot be considered to be a legally wedded wife of the man.

legal_principles.principle: Desertion requires two essential conditions: factum of separation and intention to bring cohabitation permanently to an end.

cited_cases: Bipinchandra Jaisinghbai Shah v Prabhavati

legal_principles.principle: Desertion comes to an end if the deserted spouse affirms the marriage and is ready and willing to resume married life.
legal_principles.held: Hence, it is necessary that during all the period that there has been a desertion, the deserted spouse must affirm the marriage and be ready and willing to resume married life on such conditions as may be reasonable.
cited_cases: Bipinchandra Jaisinghbai Shah v Prabhavati

legal_principles.principle: A party claiming divorce on the ground of desertion must prove that it was ready to cohabit throughout the said period.
legal_principles.held: Section 13(1)(ib) of the Hindu Marriage Act requires that a party claiming divorce on the ground of desertion should prove that it was ready to cohabit throughout the said period of 2 years prior to the filing of the petition.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party claiming divorce to prove that it was ready to cohabit throughout the said period.
The law relating to desertion is well settled by the Apex Court.
cited_cases: Bipinchandra Jaisinghbai Shah v Prabhavati

legal_principles.principle: A court must consider the evidence on record before dismissing a petition for restitution of conjugal rights.
legal_principles.held: Counsel for the appellant-husband that before the Learned Trial Court, the appellant-husband adduced oral evidence of 4(four) numbers of witnesses and the respondent-wife adduced 2(two) numbers of witnesses, but the Learned Trial Judge did not consider the evidence on record of the appellant-husband and dismissed the petition for which the interference of this Court is required.

judgments.facts_of_case: The respondent-husband filed a petition under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. He was in judicial custody at Central Jail, Ludhiana and sought time to seek fresh instructions.

legal_principles.principle: To maintain a petition at the hands of the respondent-husband under Section 9 of the Act would be an abuse of judicial process.
legal_principles.held: In such a situation, to maintain a petition at the hands of the respondent-husband under Section 9 of the Act (supra), would be abuse of judicial process and in the aforesaid circumstances calling upon the petitioner-wife to contest such petition would be a travesty of justice.

legal_principles.principle: Courts should give more weightage and consideration to the convenience of the female litigants.
legal_principles.held: The Courts are required to give more weightage and consideration to the convenience of the female litigants and transfer of legal proceedings from one Court to another should ordinarily be allowed, taking into consideration their convenience and the Courts should desist from putting female litigants under undue hardships.
cited_cases: Sumita Singh vs Kumar Sanjay, AIR 2002 SC 396
Rajani Kishor Pardeshi vs Kishor Babulal Pardeshi, (2005) 12 SCC 237

legal_principles.principle: The ends of justice should demand the transfer of suit, appeal or other proceeding.

cited_cases: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha, 2022 SCC Online SC 1199

legal_principles.principle: The Court is to consider the family condition of the wife, the custody of the minor child, economic condition of the wife, her physical health and earning capacity of the husband.
legal_principles.held: Accordingly, it is well settled that while considering the transfer of a matrimonial dispute/case, at the instance of the wife, the Court is to consider the family condition of the wife, the custody of the minor child, economic condition of the wife, her physical health and earning capacity of the husband.
cited_cases: Surinder Kaur vs Avtar Singh

outcome.final_order: The petition was transferred to a Court of competent jurisdiction at Nawanshahr.

legal_principles.held: There is no legal impediment to grant succession certificate in favour of the appellants because no any WILL executed by the deceased for estate left by him and no any application has been made to any Court for Letters of Administration.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married and the trial court granted a decree of divorce. The petitioner appealed against this decision. The respondent contracted a second marriage after the appeal was filed but before it was decided.

legal_principles.principle: When a marriage has been dissolved by a decree of divorce and either there is no right of appeal against the decree or, if there is such a right of appeal, the time for appealing has expired without an appeal having been presented, or an appeal has been presented but has been dismissed, it shall be lawful for either party to the marriage to marry again.
legal_principles.held: Sri.Dileep submitted that the present appeal against the decree of divorce was not filed on time. It was delayed by 113 days.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party seeking to set aside a decree of divorce to show that the appeal was filed within the statutory time limit.
legal_principles.held: Even though the appeal and the application for condonation of delay was filed on ..2.. 17.08.2010 and this Court ordered notice on both on 30.08.2010, the appellant did not take any steps for serving notice.

outcome.final_order: The final order was that the decree of divorce was confirmed and the respondent's second marriage was valid.

judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 2013. The wife filed a petition for divorce under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, alleging cruelty. The trial court granted the husband's petition for divorce. The wife appealed to this court.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse has a right to emotional support and care during pregnancy.
legal_principles.held: When the wife later conceived, instead of expressing joy or providing care, the husband and his mother allegedly ill-treated her both physically and mentally.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse's family members cannot drive away the other spouse from the matrimonial home.
legal_principles.held: By picking unnecessary quarrels, the husband and his mother allegedly drove her out while she was pregnant, without giving her any money.

legal_principles.principle: A spouse has a right to access their belongings and medical records during a crisis.
legal_principles.held: When the wife requested permission to take her clothes and medical records from the house, she was not permitted to enter.

outcome.final_order: The marriage was dissolved under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

judgments.case_name: S Kumara Swamy vs Smt P Mala
judgments.facts_of_case: Appellant and respondent got married in 2005. Respondent's mother interfered with their marital life. Appellant requested respondent to join the matrimonial home, but she refused. She filed a police complaint against appellant and his family members for alleged offences under IPC. The criminal case is pending.

legal_principles.principle: Mere filing of a police complaint does not amount to mental cruelty unless the jurisdictional court gives a finding that the initiation of the case is malicious and false.
legal_principles.held: In the absence of any such finding, we are of the opinion that mere filing of a police complaint ipso facto does not amount to mental cruelty.
cited_cases: RANI NARASIMHA SASTRY Vs. RANI SUNEELA RANI, (2020) 18 SCC 247

legal_principles.principle: When a person undergoes a trial in which he is acquitted of the allegation of offence under Section 498-A of IPC, it cannot be accepted that no cruelty has meted on the husband.
legal_principles.held: But when a person undergoes a trial in which he is acquitted of the allegation of offence under Section 498-A of IPC, levelled by the wife against the husband, it cannot be accepted that no cruelty has meted on the husband.
cited_cases: RAJ TALREJA Vs. KAVITA TALREJA, [(2017) 14 SCC 194]

outcome.final_order: The petition seeking dissolution of marriage was dismissed by the trial court, and this dismissal is upheld on appeal.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner is the legally wedded wife of respondent. They got married at Vizianagaram on 15.08.2024 as per Hindu rites and customs. Petitioner filed petition under Section 24 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 seeking to withdraw F.C.O.P.No.2335 of 2024 from Family Judge-Cum-V Additional District Judge, Visakhapatnam and transfer the same to Family Court at Vizianagaram.

legal_principles.principle: A transfer petition filed by a wife may be allowed if she does not have sufficient funds to visit the place where the divorce petition is filed by her husband.
legal_principles.held: By considering the fact that 'if a wife does not have sufficient funds to visit the place where the divorce petition is filed by her husband, then the transfer petition filed by the wife may be allowed.'
cited_cases: GEETA HEERA Vs HARISH CHANDER , (Year) X SCC Y

legal_principles.principle: A wife may be allowed to transfer a case from one place to another if she does not have sufficient male support.
legal_principles.held: In view of the above, it is held that 'the cardinal principle for exercise of power under Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is that the burden lies on the wife to show that she has no male support.'
cited_cases: N.C.V. Aishwarya Vs A.S.Saravana Karthik Sha^h^l

outcome.final_order: Service held sufficient. Petitioner's petition under Section 24 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 seeking to withdraw F.C.O.P.No.2335 of 2024 from Family Judge-Cum-V Additional District Judge, Visakhapatnam and transfer the same to Family Court at Vizianagaram is allowed.

legal_principles.principle: The question as to whether a reference would be necessary if a view sustaining 'not maintainable' argument is taken arises.
legal_principles.held: In the light of Dr.Rajiv Verghese case (Dr.Rajiv Verghese Vs. Rosy Chakkrammakkil Francis) reported in 2023 (1) Law Weekly 278, the question whether a reference would be necessary if a view sustaining 'not maintainable' argument is taken arises.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner and respondent were married in 2018. Respondent filed for dissolution of marriage, while petitioner filed for restitution of conjugal rights. Petitioner has to travel from Mangalore to Tiruchirappalli to contest the case.

legal_principles.principle: Maintenance being the livelihood of a child and Right to Life being an integral part of Article 21 and a Fundamental Right, the Courts are bound to interfere in such circumstances and ensure that the maintenance of the children are protected at all circumstances.
legal_principles.held: The agony of the child and its mental condition during the period of dispute between father and mother, all to be taken note of and the interim maintenance is to be ordered by the Courts even if there is no application or otherwise.

legal_principles.principle: Remedy of maintenance is a social justice as envisaged under the Constitution to prevent the child from falling into destitution or vagrant.
legal_principles.held: Therefore, even in the absence of application seeking maintenance, the Courts are bound to consider the grant of interim maintenance whenever a child is residing with the mother, who is not employed.

legal_principles.principle: Courts are bound to protect the interest of the minor children at all circumstances.
legal_principles.held: However, the interest of the minor child is of paramount importance and the Courts are bound to protect the interest of the minor children at all circumstances.

legal_principles.principle: Courts are bound to consider the grant of interim maintenance even in the absence of any application from the mother till such time the final maintenance is to be determined after adjudication.
legal_principles.held: Thus, the Family Courts or the Courts dealing with the matrimonial cases are bound to consider the grant of interim maintenance even in the absence of any application from the mother till such time the final maintenance is to be determined after adjudication.

outcome.final_order: Case transferred to Principal Subordinate Court, Tiruchirappalli to be tried along with H.M.O.P.No.248 of 2022.

legal_principles.principle: The burden is always on the person who claims herself to be the legally married wife of the person from whom she claims maintenance.
legal_principles.held: And in the case in hand, the respondent has miserably failed to prove that she is legally married with the petitioner and the same fulfill the condition for a Hindu marriage as laid down in Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

legal_principles.principle: A woman in accordance with Hindu rights with a man having a living spouse is a complete nullity in the eye of law.
legal_principles.held: (ii). That, the marriage of a woman in accordance with Hindu rights with a man having a living spouse is a complete nullity in the eye of law and therefore, she is not entitled to the benefit of Section 125 Cr.P.C.

legal_principles.principle: To be entitled for maintenance under Section 125 of the Cr.P.C., a person must prove that she is legally married with the petitioner and fulfill the condition for a Hindu marriage as laid down in Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
legal_principles.held: (v). That, to be entitled for maintenance under Section 125 of the Cr.P.C., the burden is always on the person who claims herself to be the legally married wife of the person from whom she claims maintenance. judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married and the respondent filed a divorce petition under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The trial court granted the divorce by mutual consent. The petitioner appeals against this order.

legal_principles.principle: A party's statement in court must be truthful and not a false plea to extort more money.
legal_principles.held: It is clear from the record that there is no force, fraud, threat, pressure, coercion or undue influence exercised against petitioner No.1 and she is coming up with a false plea of the same in order to extort more money from petitioner No. 2.

legal_principles.principle: A party's failure to substantiate their averments with evidence can lead to the court drawing adverse inferences.
legal_principles.held: She is simply enjoying the benefits of Rs.8 lacs which was given to her in cash at the time of recording of the statement in the first motion petition and-has not returned the same to petitioner number as is clear from the order sheet dated 23.07.2007.

outcome.final_order: The appeal is allowed and the decree of divorce is set aside.

judgments.court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
judgments.trial_court: Subordinate Court, Ottanchathiram (HMOP No.185 of 2022)
judgments.case_name: Tmt.Kavitha vs Sathyamoorthy
judgments.facts_of_case: The parties were married in 2022 and have a child. The husband filed for divorce, but the wife is unable to travel to contest due to her responsibilities as a school owner and her daughter's NEET examination. The wife also seeks maintenance for their child.

legal_principles.principle: Maintenance is the livelihood for a child, and even in cases where the wife is employed, the father has to contribute his share of maintenance.
legal_principles.held: The remedy of interim maintenance is a measure of social justice as envisaged under the Constitution to prevent the children from falling into destitution and vagrancy.

legal_principles.principle: Interim maintenance is to be granted whenever a child is to be maintained by the parents, considering the status, income, lifestyle and other mitigating factors.
legal_principles.held: The Courts cannot keep such maintenance petitions pending for a prolonged period; soon after the filing of the same, interim maintenance is to be granted.

legal_principles.principle: The domicile or citizenship of the opposite party is immaterial in a case like this, and the residence of the wife determines the question of jurisdiction.
legal_principles.held: The Hon'ble Division Bench of the High Court of Madras has observed that 'the domicile or citizenship of the opposite party is immaterial in a case like this'.

outcome.final_order: The petition for transfer was allowed, and the HMOP No.185 of 2022 was transferred from the Subordinate Court, Ottanchathiram to the Subordinate Court, Udumalapet.

legal_principles.principle: The principle of res judicata applies when the cause of action is the same and all averments are one and the same.
legal_principles.held: It was observed that all the averments in the earlier petition and the petition filed before him were one and the same, and therefore, the cause of action was also the same.

legal_principles.principle: A Family Court has exclusive jurisdiction to decide on the validity of a marriage and matrimonial status.
legal_principles.held: Under Section 7(1) Explanation (b) of the Family Courts Act, 1984, a suit or a proceeding for a declaration as to the validity of both marriage and matrimonial status of a person is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Family Court.

judgments.trial_court: Family Court, Balasore, Case No. 306 of 2019
judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner-husband filed for transfer of CP case pending in Family Court, Balasore. Respondent-wife is serving at Kolkata and has filed application for dissolution of marriage with petitioner.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party seeking transfer of a proceeding to establish that the court in seisin is not well connected with the place where the opposite party resides.
legal_principles.held: Considering the submissions made and on going through the averments taken in the application, it is clear that the opposite party has failed to make out any case for transfer.

legal_principles.principle: A court's well connection with a place is not just physical proximity, but also includes connectivity by road and rail.
legal_principles.held: Balasore is at a distance of around 25 kms from the place of her service; whereas the petitioner is residing in the district of Jajpur which is at a distance of around 110 kms from the place where the court in seisin of the proceeding which is sought to be transferred situates and that is well communicated with Balasore both by road as well as rail.

outcome.final_order: Application stands dismissed.

legal_principles.held: The Apex Court has summarized the ratio of all the cases decided earlier with respect to quashing of F.I.R./charge-sheet/criminal proceeding on the ground of settlement between the parties.

judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner and respondent were married in 2020 and have a child together. They are living separately due to misunderstandings. Respondent filed FCOP for restitution of conjugal rights before the Family Court, Vellore.

legal_principles.principle: The domicile or citizenship of the opposite party is immaterial in a case like this.
legal_principles.held: In case the marriage was solemnized under Hindu Law marital relationship is governed by the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act. Therefore, Section 19 has to be given a purposeful interpretation.

legal_principles.principle: The residence of the wife determines the question of jurisdiction.
legal_principles.held: It is the residence of the wife, which determines the question of jurisdiction, in case the proceeding was initiated at the instance of the wife.

legal_principles.principle: The objects and reasons which prompted the parliament to incorporate a provision have to be taken note of.
legal_principles.held: While considering a provision like Section 19 (iii-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, the objects and reasons which prompted the parliament to incorporate such a provision has also to be taken note of.

legal_principles.principle: The difficulty faced by the wife in traveling or staying at a distant place is a relevant factor.
legal_principles.held: Experience is the best teacher. The Government found the difficulties faced by women in the matter of initiation of matrimonial proceedings.

outcome.final_order: Petition for transfer is allowed and FCOP No.85 of 2022 is transferred to the file of Sub Court, Arakkonam.

The marriage was solemnised on 20.03.1965 and they lived together till Madhavan Nair's death on 28.8.2009. After his death, petitioner applied for family pension as his heir but it was rejected stating that Janaki Amma is the next of kin.

legal_principles.principle: A second marriage contracted during the subsistence of the first marriage would be void in law.
legal_principles.held: The claim of the daughter of the petitioner for any share in the family pension was also disputed by the 2nd respondent. It was further stated that the 1st respondent herein was the nominee of Sri.Madhavan Nair in all his service records.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the party claiming to be the legally wedded wife to prove the same.
legal_principles.held: It was further stated that the 1st respondent herein was the nominee of Sri.Madhavan Nair in all his service records.

outcome.final_order: The court declared that the petitioner is the legally wedded wife of late K.Madhavan Nair and entitled to family pension as his heir.

judgments.trial_court: Judicial Magistrate No. 2, Salem, C.C. No. 164 of 2000
judgments.case_name: T.P. Ravichandran And Ors. vs S. Padma
judgments.facts_of_case: Marriage between husband and wife was solemnized in 1996. Husband approached the Sub Court for divorce on grounds of cruelty and adultery. Ex-parte decree was passed. Wife suffered a decree for divorce. Husband married another lady.

legal_principles.principle: A decree of divorce, whether ex-parte or otherwise, is a valid one and subsists till it is set aside.
legal_principles.held: As seen from the Marriage Certificate, the first petitioner married another lady on 15.11.1998 i.e. when the decree for divorce, whether it is ex-parte or otherwise, which is a valid one, was in subsistence.
cited_cases: Gopal Divedi v. Prabha Divedi, (2002) M.L.J. (Crl.) 726

legal_principles.principle: When a husband has married another lady during the period when his previous marriage was subsisting, but the decree of divorce was in force, he cannot be convicted for bigamy.
legal_principles.held: The Apex Court came to the conclusion that the first marriage was not subsisting, in view of the ex-parte decree, which continued to be in force on the date of the second marriage and therefore, the appellant therein, cannot, possibly, be convicted for the offence under Section 494 IPC.
cited_cases: Gopal Divedi v. Prabha Divedi, (2002) M.L.J. (Crl.) 726

outcome.final_order: Ex-parte decree of divorce not set aside till 22.1.1999 or 25.1.1999

legal_principles.principle: The term 'spouse' in Clause (a) of Section 4 would apply to a spouse married under the Hindu Marriage Act as well.
legal_principles.held: We cannot read into this section something which is not there. Moreover, if we accept this interpretation it would lead to disastrous results.

judgments.case_name: Upanita Das v. Arunava Das
judgments.facts_of_case: The wife filed an application under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act for maintenance pendente lite. She prayed for Rs. 30,000/- per month and Rs.75,000/- as litigation cost. The trial court allowed 1/5th of the husband's income (Rs.60,000/- per month) as maintenance pendente lite.

legal_principles.principle: The object behind granting maintenance is to ensure that the dependent spouse was not reduced to destitution or vagrancy on account of failure of the marriage and not as a punishment to the other spouse.
legal_principles.held: So viewed, it is possible to be selective in picking out that interpretation out of two alternatives which advances the cause – the cause of the derelicts.
cited_cases: Captain Ramesh Chander Kaushal v. Mrs. Veena Kaushal and ors., (1978) 4 SCC 70

legal_principles.principle: The quantum of maintenance should be determined by considering the status of the parties, reasonable wants of the claimant, independent income and property of the claimant, number of persons the non-applicant has to maintain, amount that aids the applicant to live in a similar lifestyle as he/she enjoyed in the matrimonial home, non-applicant's liabilities, payment capacity of the non-applicant, cost of litigation, and amount awarded under Section 125 Cr.PC.
legal_principles.held: Apart from the aforesaid factors enumerated hereinabove, certain additional factors would also be relevant for determining the quantum of maintenance payable.
cited_cases: Rajnesh v. Neha and ors., (2020)

outcome.final_order: The final order is not specified in this excerpt.

legal_principles.held: The High Court in exercise of power under sections 14 and 21 of the Hindu Marriage Act , 1955 has framed Rules. Under Rule 2(7)(e)(2) of the Rules, in a petition seeking dissolution of marriage on the ground of adultery, the date and place of the adultery and the name and address of the person with whom the adultery was committed by the respondent is required to be stated.

legal_principles.principle: A person whose reputation is likely to be affected by a finding recorded in a suit should have an opportunity to defend their reputation before such a finding is recorded.
legal_principles.held: The aforesaid Rule [Rule 5] enjoins a duty on the Court to issue notice to the respondent and co-respondent, if any. The principle is that such a person should have an opportunity to defend his reputation before such a finding is recorded.

cited_cases: Arun Kumar Agrawal, supra

legal_principles.principle: A Hindu marriage is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living.

legal_principles.principle: Consent to divorce must not be obtained through fraud or coercion.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the respondent to show that she was not well and taking treatment at the relevant point of time.
legal_principles.held: Though the respondent in the affidavit has alleged that she was having leg joints issue and his father was also taking treatment, but she has not elaborated anything further. Admittedly, the respondent has not produced any iota of material or evidence to show that the respondent and her father were not well and were taking treatment at the relevant point of time.

legal_principles.principle: A party's failure to produce evidence to support their claim can lead to the dismissal of the petition.
legal_principles.held: The respondent has not shown any valid reason to condone the delay of more than 1300 days and that since the petition is not having any merits, the same is liable to be dismissed.

outcome.final_order: Civil Revision Petition is dismissed

judgments.case_name: Veena Anand vs State Of H.P. And Another

parties.respondent_defendant: State of H.P. and another — husband and his family members

judgments.facts_of_case: Informant Dr. Priyanka Lakhanpal filed a complaint against her husband and his family members for dowry harassment.

legal_principles.principle: A complaint can be quashed where the allegations made in the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out the case alleged against the accused.
legal_principles.held: For this purpose, the complaint has to be examined as a whole, but without examining the merits of the allegations. Neither a detailed inquiry nor a meticulous analysis of the material nor an assessment of the reliability or genuineness of the allegations in the complaint is warranted while examining prayer for quashing a complaint.
cited_cases: State of Bihar v. Rajendra Agrawalla [(1996) 8 SCC 164: 1996 SCC (Cri) 628]

legal_principles.principle: A complaint may also be quashed where it is a clear abuse of the process of the court, as when the criminal proceeding is found to have been initiated with mala fides/malice for wreaking vengeance or to cause harm, or where the allegations are absurd and inherently improbable.
legal_principles.held: The power to quash shall not, however, be used to stifle or scuttle a legitimate prosecution. The power should be used sparingly and with abundant caution.
cited_cases: State of Bihar v. Rajendra Agrawalla [(1996) 8 SCC 164: 1996 SCC (Cri) 628]

legal_principles.principle: The complaint is not required to verbatim reproduce the legal ingredients of the offence alleged. If the necessary factual foundation is laid in the complaint, merely on the ground that a few ingredients have not been stated in detail, the proceedings should not be quashed.
legal_principles.held: Quashing of the complaint is warranted only where the complaint is so bereft of even the basic facts which are necessary for making out the offence.
cited_cases: State of Bihar v. Rajendra Agrawalla [(1996) 8 SCC 164: 1996 SCC (Cri) 628]

legal_principles.principle: A given set of facts may make out: (a) purely a civil wrong; (b) purely a criminal offence; or (c) a civil wrong as also a criminal offence.
legal_principles.held: A commercial transaction or a contractual dispute, apart from furnishing a cause of action for seeking remedy in civil law, may also involve a criminal offence. As the nature and scope of a civil proceeding are different from a criminal proceeding, the mere fact that the complaint relates to a commercial transaction or breach of contract, for which a civil remedy is available or has been availed, is not by itself a ground to quash the criminal proceedings.
cited_cases: State of Bihar v. Rajendra Agrawalla [(1996) 8 SCC 164: 1996 SCC (Cri) 628]

outcome.final_order: The summoning order dated 18.9.2020 was quashed.

use_for_drafting: drafting a petition for quashing a summoning order
advising on divorce proceedings in the High Court
assisting with a complaint filed under IPC

legal_principles.held: On the other, those criminal cases having overwhelmingly and pre-dominantly civil character, particularly those arising out of commercial transactions or arising out of matrimonial relationship or family disputes should be quashed when the parties have resolved their entire disputes among themselves.

legal_principles.principle: It is not safe to leave the crime-doer only because he and the victim have settled the dispute amicably or that the victim has been paid compensation, yet certain crimes have been made compoundable in law, with or without the permission of the court.

judgments.facts_of_case: The wife filed a petition for dissolution of marriage under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The husband lost before both courts below and appealed to challenge the orders.

legal_principles.principle: The burden lies on the petitioner to establish his or her plea that the respondent had meted out cruelty.
legal_principles.held: normally the burden lies on the petitioner to establish his or her plea that the respondent had meted out cruelty and that the standard of proof required in matrimonial cases under the Act is not to establish the charge of cruelty beyond reasonable doubt but merely one of weighing the various probabilities to find out whether the preponderance is in favour of the existence of the said fact alleged.
cited_cases: Dr. N.G. Dastane v. Mrs. S. Dastane, AIR (1975) SC 1534

legal_principles.principle: Mental cruelty can broadly be defined as that conduct which inflicts upon the other party such mental pain and suffering as would make it not possible for that party to live with the other.
legal_principles.held: mental cruelty in Section 13(1) (i-a) can broadly be defined as that conduct which inflicts upon the other party such mental pain and suffering as would make it not possible for that party to live with the other and the parties cannot reasonably also be expected to live together or that the wronged party cannot reasonably be asked to put up with such conduct and continue to live with the other party.
cited_cases: V. Bhagat v. D. Bhagat (Mrs.), [1994] 1 SCC 337

outcome.final_order: The final court order granted dissolution of marriage and divorce on the ground of cruelty.

legal_principles.significance: HIGH — to determine the applicability of Hindu Marriage Act

legal_principles.principle: Legislative intent should not be reduced to futility by a bare mechanical interpretation.
legal_principles.held: The Apex Court held that a bare mechanical interpretation of the words and application of a legislative intent devoid of concept of purpose will reduce most of the remedial and beneficent legislation to futility.
cited_cases: Organo Chemical Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1979 SC 1803
legal_principles.significance: MEDIUM — to emphasize the importance of considering legislative intent

outcome.final_order: The court held that the Hindu Marriage Act applies to a Hindu outside India if he is a Hindu domiciled in India, and not just those with permanent residence in India.

The wife moved an interim application under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act seeking maintenance. The trial court allowed the application and directed the husband to pay Rs.25,000/- per month each to his wife and minor child.

legal_principles.principle: The court should not mechanically entertain and allow an application without considering vital aspects.
legal_principles.held: hereby, the appellant has brought this appeal on the ground that the IV Additional Family Court, Chennai ought not to have mechanically entertained and allowed the Interim Application filed under Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, without considering various vital aspects raised by the appellant.

legal_principles.principle: A court should not pass an order that a party cannot comply with.
legal_principles.held: Therefore, the impugned order passed by the Family Court to pay Rs.25,000/- per month each to the wife and the minor child is virtually unenforceable as the appellant has been paying house rent allowance, transport allowance, utility allowance and in addition thereto he has been undertaking flight expenses from Dubai to Chennai for the sake of proceedings pending before this Court.

outcome.final_order: The final order is that the appeal against the fair and decretal order dated 27.11.2019 passed by the IV Additional Family Court, Chennai is dismissed.

legal_principles.principle: The Family Court can only assume jurisdiction if there is a dispute between the parties to a marriage with respect to their marital status, divorce, restitution of conjugal rights, judicial separation, child custody, maintenance, or property sharing.
legal_principles.held: But, in no event, the Family Court can have jurisdiction if the above dispute is absent. By no stretch of imagination, can the Family Court assume jurisdiction, if there is a dispute between the brothers, sisters, mothers, fathers etc. concerning property and the case on hand being one such, the Family Court had clearly no jurisdiction.
cited_cases: P. Srihari (supra)

legal_principles.principle: The Family Court's jurisdiction is limited to suits and proceedings between the parties to a marriage with respect to their property or of either of them.
legal_principles.held: A plain reading of the provisions would manifest that for maintaining a suit or proceeding of the nature mentioned in Explanation (c) sub-section (1) of Section 7 of the Act, 1984, the suit or proceeding has to be between the parties to a marriage with respect to the property of the parties or of either of them.

legal_principles.principle: A child of a voidable marriage shall be deemed to be the legitimate child of the parties if at the date of the decree it had been dissolved instead of being annulled.
legal_principles.held: Where a decree of nullity is granted in respect of a voidable marriage under section 12, any child begotten or conceived before the decree is made, who would have been the legitimate child of the parties to the marriage if at the date of the decree it had been dissolved instead of being annulled, shall be deemed to be their legitimate child.

judgments.facts_of_case: Marriage between petitioner and respondent was solemnized on 28.4.2015. Parties cohabited together cordially for some time but disputes cropped up resulting in institution of cross-cases by both sides.

legal_principles.principle: Statutory period of six months for grant of divorce by way of mutual consent can be waived when there is no possibility of rapprochement and the marriage has broken beyond repair.
legal_principles.held: Since both the parties are living separately for the last many years and they have been litigating with each other, statutory period of six months as envisaged under Section 13B of the Act for grant of divorce by way of mutual consent, can be waived, especially when there is no possibility of rapprochement of the parties and marriage has broken beyond repair.
cited_cases: Veena vs. State (Government of NCT of Delhi), (2011)14 SCC 614
Priyanka Khanna v. Amit Khanna, (2011) 15 SCC 612
use_in: divorce cases where parties are living separately and have no possibility of rapprochement

legal_principles.principle: When a marriage has broken down in a very nasty manner, there is absolutely no possibility of a rapprochement between the couple even if the matter was to be adjourned for a period of six months.
legal_principles.held: We also see from the record that the first litigation had been filed by the respondent husband on 2.6.2006 and a petition for divorce had also been filed by him in the year, 2007. We therefore, feel that it would be in the interest of justice that the period of six months should be waived in view of the above facts.
cited_cases: Priyanka Khanna v. Amit Khanna, (2011) 15 SCC 612
use_in: divorce cases where the marriage has broken down in a nasty manner

judgments.trial_court: Family Court, HMA Petition No. 262-S/3 of 2019/16
judgments.case_name: Arun Sharma vs Neena Devi
judgments.facts_of_case: Petitioner sought dissolution of marriage with respondent on ground of cruelty. Respondent left matrimonial house without intimation. A son was born out of wedlock.

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional.
legal_principles.held: The cruelty may be mental or physical. It may be intentional or unintentional.
cited_cases: Shobha Rani Vs. Madhukar Reddi, (1988) 1 SCC 105

legal_principles.principle: The impact of cruel treatment on the mind of the spouse must be considered.
legal_principles.held: Second, the impact of such treatment on the mind of the spouse. Whether it caused reasonable apprehension that it would be harmful or injurious to live with the other.
cited_cases: Shobha Rani Vs. Madhukar Reddi, (1988) 1 SCC 105

legal_principles.principle: Cruelty may not be established solely by the impact of the conduct, but also by the nature of the conduct itself.
legal_principles.held: There may, however, be cases where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal. Then the impact or the injurious effect on the other spouse need not be enquired into or considered.
cited_cases: Shobha Rani Vs. Madhukar Reddi, (1988) 1 SCC 105

legal_principles.principle: The court should not import its own notions of life and should consider the type of life the parties are accustomed to.
legal_principles.held: Therefore, when a spouse makes complaint about the treatment of cruelty by the partner in life or relations, the court should not search for standard in life. A set of facts stigmatised as cruelty in one case may not be so in another case.
cited_cases: Shobha Rani Vs. Madhukar Reddi, (1988) 1 SCC 105

outcome.final_order: Order dated 09.09.2021 set aside and petition allowed.
